title: Rewriting an engine extension without changing a token
subtitle: Porting a GPU serving layer from Python to native C++ with bit-identical output, and proving every remaining line of Python was required

stats.label: exact-mode parity cells bitwise; 12 of 12 hybrid
Python files in the release payload
lines of C++ in 361 engine files

lede: ActiveKV began life as Python inside vLLM. That was the right way to find out whether the design worked and the wrong way to deliver it: the per-token path was slow, and the product logic sat in readable source. I moved the whole runtime to native C++ in under three weeks. In every parity cell the output was bit-identical, and a line-by-line audit cites the exact framework contract behind the one place Python still dispatches. A port like this fails in two ways. It changes behaviour, which in an inference engine means a different token somewhere in a long generation that nobody notices until a customer does.
quote: A framework interface requiring a Python function does not mean the implementation inside that function must be Python.
evidence: C++ and native ports with parity proof: a vLLM extension moved from Python to native C++ with 13 of 13 exact parity cells bitwise and 12 of 12 hybrid.
vLLM internals: a runtime layer inside vLLM's scheduler, worker and attention backend ported without changing those interfaces, 77,000 lines of C++ in 361 engine files.
Python and C++ interoperability: an async protocol the defence said needed Python, implemented natively through the interpreter's C API.
Technical leadership of agent teams: a seven-criterion definition of done and independent QA agents per module lane, with 0 Python files in the release payload.
Code review policy for native boundaries: an intake review that rejects new Python modules, Python imports from C++ and per-step Python callbacks on the native path.
author: Corey James
